# stopcock

> Fast, composable TypeScript packages for functional programming, dates, async work, HTTP, state, diffing, linear algebra, automatic differentiation, signal processing, color, SVG, and image processing.

Packages are independently installable under the `@stopcock` scope.

## Install

```bash
bun add @stopcock/fp
```

---
# Algebra and ordering

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/algebra/

Eq, Hash, Ord, Semigroup, Monoid, Group, and Ordering

The algebra modules are small plain objects and functions. They do not require
classes, higher-kinded-type emulation, or a runtime typeclass registry.

Eq, Hash, and Ord expose 16 dual operations. The [complete dual-call
catalogue](/api/modules#complete-dual-call-catalogue) shows both call shapes for
each one.

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as Eq from '@stopcock/fp/eq'
import * as Hash from '@stopcock/fp/hash'
import * as Ord from '@stopcock/fp/ord'
import * as Semigroup from '@stopcock/fp/semigroup'
import * as Monoid from '@stopcock/fp/monoid'
import * as Group from '@stopcock/fp/group'
```

## Equality

```ts
const pointEq = Eq.struct<Point>({
  x: Eq.number,
  y: Eq.number,
})

pointEq.equals({ x: 1, y: 2 }, { x: 1, y: 2 }) // true
```

`Eq.deep` is cycle-safe for dense arrays and plain records. Dates, maps, sets,
regular expressions, promises, and class instances are atomic unless you
provide a domain-specific instance.

## Hashing

Hash instances provide deterministic integer hashes and compose over common
containers:

```ts
const pointHash = Hash.struct<Point>({
  x: Hash.number,
  y: Hash.number,
})
```

Use compatible `Eq` and `Hash` instances whenever a hashed collection relies on
both.

## Ordering

```ts
const byAge = Ord.contramap(Ord.number, (user: User) => user.age)
const byAgeInPipe = pipe(
  Ord.number,
  Ord.contramap((user: User) => user.age),
)
const byName = pipe(
  Ord.string,
  Ord.contramap((user: User) => user.name),
)
const byAgeThenName = Ord.combine(byAge, byName)
const byAgeThenNameInPipe = pipe(byAge, Ord.combine(byName))

users.toSorted(byAgeThenName.compare)
```

`contramap` and `combine` accept their complete argument lists directly or
return a data-last operation when the instance argument is omitted.

The `ordering` module contains the `-1 | 0 | 1` primitives used by `Ord`.

## Combining values

```ts
const total = Semigroup.numberSum.combine(2, 3)
const all = Monoid.booleanAll.combineAll([true, true, false])
const delta = Group.numberSum.subtract(10, 3)
```

- A `Semigroup<A>` combines two `A` values.
- A `Monoid<A>` adds an identity value and folds empty collections.
- A `Group<A>` adds inversion/removal.

Instances are ordinary values, so application-specific instances are easy to
create and test.

---
# A (Array)

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/array/

Filter, map, sort, group, and 30+ array functions for pipe

The array module has 128 dual operations. `A.fn(arr, ...)` runs direct
data-first, while `A.fn(...)(arr)` is the curried data-last form used by
`pipe(arr, A.fn(...))`. The [complete dual-call
catalogue](/api/modules#complete-dual-call-catalogue) lists every pair.
Streaming operators such as `map`, `filter`,
`flatMap`, `take`, `drop`, `takeWhile`, and `dropWhile` can be fused into a
single loop by the separate build-time [`@stopcock/fp-compiler`](/concepts/fusion)
plugin. Plain `pipe` at runtime never fuses on its own; it just calls each
step in order. Terminal folds, accessor terminals, and materializing
operations have different boundaries in what the compiler can fuse.

## Accessors

```ts
head<A>(arr: readonly A[]): Option<A>
last<A>(arr: readonly A[]): Option<A>
first<A>(arr: readonly A[]): Option<A> // alias for head
headOrUndefined<A>(arr: readonly A[]): A | undefined
lastOrUndefined<A>(arr: readonly A[]): A | undefined
headNonEmpty<A>(arr: readonly [A, ...A[]]): A
lastNonEmpty<A>(arr: readonly [A, ...A[]]): A
tail<A>(arr: readonly A[]): A[]           // all except first
init<A>(arr: readonly A[]): A[]           // all except last
length<A>(arr: readonly A[]): number
isEmpty<A>(arr: readonly A[]): boolean
```

`head`, `last`, `length`, and `isEmpty` are accessor terminals: the compiler
can treat them as the last step of a fused loop. Option-returning names are
the default; `*OrUndefined` is the explicit JavaScript interop escape hatch.

## Transforms

```ts
map<A, B>(arr: readonly A[], f: (a: A) => B): B[]
map<A, B>(f: (a: A) => B): (arr: readonly A[]) => B[]
mapWithIndex<A, B>(arr: readonly A[], f: (a: A, i: number) => B): B[]
mapWithIndex<A, B>(f: (a: A, i: number) => B): (arr: readonly A[]) => B[]
filter<A>(arr: readonly A[], pred: (a: A) => boolean): A[]
filter<A>(pred: (a: A) => boolean): (arr: readonly A[]) => A[]
filterWithIndex<A>(arr: readonly A[], pred: (a: A, i: number) => boolean): A[]
filterWithIndex<A>(pred: (a: A, i: number) => boolean): (arr: readonly A[]) => A[]
flatMap<A, B>(arr: readonly A[], f: (a: A) => B[]): B[]
flatMap<A, B>(f: (a: A) => B[]): (arr: readonly A[]) => B[]
reduce<A, B>(arr: readonly A[], f: (acc: B, a: A) => B, init: B): B
reduce<A, B>(f: (acc: B, a: A) => B, init: B): (arr: readonly A[]) => B
reduceRight<A, B>(arr: readonly A[], f: (acc: B, a: A) => B, init: B): B
reduceRight<A, B>(f: (acc: B, a: A) => B, init: B): (arr: readonly A[]) => B
scan<A, B>(arr: readonly A[], f: (acc: B, a: A) => B, init: B): B[]
scan<A, B>(f: (acc: B, a: A) => B, init: B): (arr: readonly A[]) => B[]
forEach<A>(arr: readonly A[], f: (a: A) => void): void
forEach<A>(f: (a: A) => void): (arr: readonly A[]) => void
forEachWithIndex<A>(arr: readonly A[], f: (a: A, i: number) => void): void
forEachWithIndex<A>(f: (a: A, i: number) => void): (arr: readonly A[]) => void
```

`map`, `mapWithIndex`, `filter`, `filterWithIndex`, and `flatMap` are the
streaming steps the compiler can fuse into one loop. `reduce` is a terminal
fold. `forEach` is a terminal side-effect traversal. `scan` returns an
intermediate array of every running value.

## Ordering

```ts
sort(arr: readonly number[]): number[]
sortBy<A>(arr: readonly A[], cmp: (a: A, b: A) => number): A[]
sortBy<A>(cmp: (a: A, b: A) => number): (arr: readonly A[]) => A[]
reverse<A>(arr: readonly A[]): A[]
```

Materialization boundaries: they need the whole array before they can
produce anything. `sort` and `sortBy` always run a full sort; a following
`take` does not get a bounded top-k shortcut.

## Slicing

```ts
take<A>(arr: readonly A[], n: number): A[]
take(n: number): <A>(arr: readonly A[]) => A[]
drop<A>(arr: readonly A[], n: number): A[]
drop(n: number): <A>(arr: readonly A[]) => A[]
takeWhile<A>(arr: readonly A[], pred: (a: A) => boolean): A[]
takeWhile<A>(pred: (a: A) => boolean): (arr: readonly A[]) => A[]
dropWhile<A>(arr: readonly A[], pred: (a: A) => boolean): A[]
dropWhile<A>(pred: (a: A) => boolean): (arr: readonly A[]) => A[]
chunk<A>(arr: readonly A[], n: number): A[][]
chunk(n: number): <A>(arr: readonly A[]) => A[][]
slidingWindow<A>(arr: readonly A[], n: number): A[][]
slidingWindow(n: number): <A>(arr: readonly A[]) => A[][]
aperture<A>(arr: readonly A[], n: number): A[][]
aperture(n: number): <A>(arr: readonly A[]) => A[][]
```

`take`, `drop`, `takeWhile`, and `dropWhile` are streaming steps the
compiler can fuse. `take` and `takeWhile` can stop the loop early.

## Search

```ts
find<A>(arr: readonly A[], pred: (a: A) => boolean): Option<A>
find<A>(pred: (a: A) => boolean): (arr: readonly A[]) => Option<A>
findIndex<A>(arr: readonly A[], pred: (a: A) => boolean): Option<number>
findIndex<A>(pred: (a: A) => boolean): (arr: readonly A[]) => Option<number>
findOrUndefined<A>(arr: readonly A[], pred: (a: A) => boolean): A | undefined
findOrUndefined<A>(pred: (a: A) => boolean): (arr: readonly A[]) => A | undefined
findIndexOrUndefined<A>(arr: readonly A[], pred: (a: A) => boolean): number | undefined
findIndexOrUndefined<A>(pred: (a: A) => boolean): (arr: readonly A[]) => number | undefined
every<A>(arr: readonly A[], pred: (a: A) => boolean): boolean
every<A>(pred: (a: A) => boolean): (arr: readonly A[]) => boolean
some<A>(arr: readonly A[], pred: (a: A) => boolean): boolean
some<A>(pred: (a: A) => boolean): (arr: readonly A[]) => boolean
includes<A>(arr: readonly A[], value: A): boolean
includes<A>(value: A): (arr: readonly A[]) => boolean
```

`find`, `every`, and `some` are terminal predicates/searches: the compiler
can run them as the last step of a fused loop and bail out early.

## Deduplication

```ts
uniq<A>(arr: readonly A[]): A[]
uniqBy<A, B>(arr: readonly A[], f: (a: A) => B): A[]
uniqBy<A, B>(f: (a: A) => B): (arr: readonly A[]) => A[]
```

Deduplication needs seen-value state and returns a materialized array.

## Set operations

```ts
intersection<A>(a: readonly A[], b: readonly A[]): A[]
intersection<A>(b: readonly A[]): (a: readonly A[]) => A[]
union<A>(a: readonly A[], b: readonly A[]): A[]
union<A>(b: readonly A[]): (a: readonly A[]) => A[]
difference<A>(a: readonly A[], b: readonly A[]): A[]
difference<A>(b: readonly A[]): (a: readonly A[]) => A[]
symmetricDifference<A>(a: readonly A[], b: readonly A[]): A[]
symmetricDifference<A>(b: readonly A[]): (a: readonly A[]) => A[]
```

## Combinators

```ts
zip<A, B>(a: readonly A[], b: readonly B[]): [A, B][]
zip<B>(b: readonly B[]): <A>(a: readonly A[]) => [A, B][]
zipWith<A, B, C>(a: readonly A[], b: readonly B[], f: (a: A, b: B) => C): C[]
zipWith<A, B, C>(b: readonly B[], f: (a: A, b: B) => C): (a: readonly A[]) => C[]
xprod<A, B>(a: readonly A[], b: readonly B[]): [A, B][]
xprod<B>(b: readonly B[]): <A>(a: readonly A[]) => [A, B][]
groupBy<A>(arr: readonly A[], f: (a: A) => string): Record<string, A[]>
groupBy<A>(f: (a: A) => string): (arr: readonly A[]) => Record<string, A[]>
partition<A>(arr: readonly A[], pred: (a: A) => boolean): [A[], A[]]
partition<A>(pred: (a: A) => boolean): (arr: readonly A[]) => [A[], A[]]
intersperse<A>(arr: readonly A[], sep: A): A[]
intersperse<A>(sep: A): (arr: readonly A[]) => A[]
flatten<A>(arr: readonly A[][]): A[]
transpose<A>(arr: readonly A[][]): A[][]
```

`groupBy` is a materialization boundary because it needs the whole grouped result.

## Mutation (immutable)

```ts
adjust<A>(arr: readonly A[], index: number, f: (a: A) => A): A[]
adjust<A>(index: number, f: (a: A) => A): (arr: readonly A[]) => A[]
update<A>(arr: readonly A[], index: number, value: A): A[]
update<A>(index: number, value: A): (arr: readonly A[]) => A[]
insert<A>(arr: readonly A[], index: number, value: A): A[]
insert<A>(index: number, value: A): (arr: readonly A[]) => A[]
remove<A>(arr: readonly A[], index: number, count: number): A[]
remove(index: number, count: number): <A>(arr: readonly A[]) => A[]
```

All return new arrays.

## Constructors

```ts
range(start: number, end: number): number[]
repeat<A>(value: A, n: number): A[]
repeat<A>(n: number): (value: A) => A[]
times<A>(f: (i: number) => A, n: number): A[]
times(n: number): <A>(f: (i: number) => A) => A[]
unfold<A, B>(f: (seed: B) => [A, B] | undefined, seed: B): A[]
unfold<A, B>(seed: B): (f: (seed: B) => [A, B] | undefined) => A[]
```

## Examples

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as A from '@stopcock/fp/array'

type Product = {
  name: string
  price: number
  category: string
  inStock: boolean
}

// the compiler can fuse filter -> map -> take into one loop;
// plain pipe just runs each step in order
const deals = pipe(
  products,
  A.filter((p: Product) => p.inStock && p.price < 50),
  A.map((p) => ({ name: p.name, price: p.price })),
  A.take(10),
)

// group + count
const byCategory = A.groupBy(products, (p: Product) => p.category)
// { electronics: [...], clothing: [...] }

// rolling total
A.scan([100, 200, 150, 300], (acc, x) => acc + x, 0)
// [0, 100, 300, 450, 750]

// remove duplicates by key
const uniqueCustomers = pipe(
  orders,
  A.uniqBy((o: { customerId: string }) => o.customerId),
)

// set operations
const newUsers = A.difference(allUsers, existingUsers)
const commonTags = pipe(tagsA, A.intersection(tagsB))

// batch processing
const batches = A.chunk(records, 100)
```

---
# B (Boolean)

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/boolean/

not, and, or, ifElse. Boolean combinators for pipe

All three dual Boolean operations appear with both shapes in the [complete
dual-call catalogue](/api/modules#complete-dual-call-catalogue).

```ts
not_(a: boolean): boolean
and_(a: boolean, b: boolean): boolean
and_(b: boolean): (a: boolean) => boolean
or_(a: boolean, b: boolean): boolean
or_(b: boolean): (a: boolean) => boolean
ifElse<A>(cond: boolean, onTrue: () => A, onFalse: () => A): A
ifElse<A>(onTrue: () => A, onFalse: () => A): (cond: boolean) => A
```

Trailing underscores avoid colliding with JS reserved words.

## Examples

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as B from '@stopcock/fp/boolean'

pipe(true, B.not_) // false
B.and_(true, false) // false, direct data-first
pipe(true, B.and_(false)) // false, curried data-last
pipe(
  false,
  B.ifElse(
    () => 'yes',
    () => 'no',
  ),
) // 'no'

// toggle a feature flag
const toggled = pipe(isEnabled, B.not_)

// both conditions must hold
const canAccess = pipe(isAdmin, B.and_(isActive))
```

---
# Dict migration

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/dict/

Dict was replaced by Record in @stopcock/fp 2.0

The 1.x `D` namespace and `/dict` subpath were removed. Use the property-key
aware record module:

```diff
- import { D } from '@stopcock/fp'
+ import * as Record from '@stopcock/fp/record'

- D.toEntries(values)
+ Record.entries(values)
```

The new module includes immutable `get`, `set`, `remove`, `modify`, `update`,
`map`, `filter`, `filterMap`, `mapKeys`, `merge`, `pick`, `omit`, `partition`,
`reduce`, and equality operations. Bulk construction and transforms have
explicit `fromEntriesInto`, `mapInto`, and `filterInto` forms.

Record has 20 dual operations. See their paired direct and curried shapes in
the [complete dual-call catalogue](/api/modules#complete-dual-call-catalogue).

Unlike the old string-only `Dict` vocabulary, records preserve enumerable
`PropertyKey` values, including symbols.

---
# G (Guards)

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/guards/

isString, isNumber, isNil, isDeepEqual and more. Runtime type guards with TypeScript predicates

Runtime type checks that narrow the TypeScript type.

The ten dual guard operations are listed with both public call shapes in the
[complete dual-call catalogue](/api/modules#complete-dual-call-catalogue).

```ts
type Guard<A> = Refinement<unknown, A>
```

## Type checks

```ts
isString(x: unknown): x is string
isNumber(x: unknown): x is number
isFiniteNumber(x: unknown): x is number
isNonBlankString(x: unknown): x is string
isBoolean(x: unknown): x is boolean
isBigInt(x: unknown): x is bigint
isSymbol(x: unknown): x is symbol
isFunction(x: unknown): x is Function
isDate(x: unknown): x is Date
isError(x: unknown): x is Error
isPromise(x: unknown): x is Promise<unknown>
isArray(x: unknown): x is unknown[]
isObjectType(x: unknown): x is object
isPlainObject(x: unknown): x is Record<string, unknown>
isArrayOf<A>(value: unknown, guard: Guard<A>): value is A[]
isArrayOf<A>(guard: Guard<A>): Guard<A[]>
isRecordOf<A>(value: unknown, guard: Guard<A>): value is Record<string, A>
isRecordOf<A>(guard: Guard<A>): Guard<Record<string, A>>
```

`isPlainObject` rejects arrays and class instances. `isObjectType` is just a `typeof` check.
`isRecordOf` accepts only plain objects and checks every own enumerable string-keyed value. Empty
arrays and records are valid because every contained value satisfies the supplied guard.

## Nullability

```ts
isNil(x: unknown): x is null | undefined
isNotNil<T>(x: T | null | undefined): x is T
isNull(x: unknown): x is null
isUndefined(x: unknown): x is undefined
isNullish(x: unknown): x is null | undefined
isNonNull<T>(x: T | null): x is T
isNonNullish<T>(x: T | null | undefined): x is T
isDefined<T>(x: T | undefined): x is T
```

## Equality

```ts
isDeepEqual(a: unknown, b: unknown): boolean
isDeepEqual(b: unknown): (a: unknown) => boolean
isShallowEqual(a: unknown, b: unknown): boolean
isShallowEqual(b: unknown): (a: unknown) => boolean
isStrictEqual(a: unknown, b: unknown): boolean
isStrictEqual(b: unknown): (a: unknown) => boolean
```

## Other

```ts
isEmpty(x: unknown): boolean
isEmptyish(x: unknown): boolean        // null, undefined, or empty
isTruthy(x: unknown): boolean
is<T>(val: unknown, ctor: new (...args: any[]) => T): val is T
is<T>(ctor: new (...args: any[]) => T): (val: unknown) => val is T
propIs<T>(obj: Record<string, unknown>, ctor: new (...args: any[]) => T, prop: string): boolean
propIs<T>(ctor: new (...args: any[]) => T, prop: string): (obj: Record<string, unknown>) => boolean
```

## Examples

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as A from '@stopcock/fp/array'
import * as G from '@stopcock/fp/guard'

// narrow unknown API data
const data: unknown[] = [1, 'hello', null, { a: 1 }]
data.filter(G.isNumber) // [1], typed as number[]
data.filter(G.isNonNullish) // [1, 'hello', { a: 1 }]

// validate form field
if (G.isString(input) && !G.isEmpty(input)) {
  submit(input)
}

// filter mixed arrays in pipe
pipe(
  rawValues,
  A.filter(G.isNumber), // unknown[] → number[]
  A.filter((n) => n > 0),
)

// deep equality check
G.isDeepEqual({ a: [1, 2] }, { a: [1, 2] }) // true
pipe({ a: [1, 2] }, G.isDeepEqual({ a: [1, 2] })) // true

// check class instance
G.is(new Date(), Date) // true: data-first
pipe('2024-01-01', G.is(Date)) // false: data-last

const numbers = G.isArrayOf(G.isFiniteNumber)
numbers([1, 2, 3]) // true
G.isArrayOf([1, Number.NaN], G.isFiniteNumber) // false: data-first

const labels = G.isRecordOf(G.isNonBlankString)
labels({ primary: 'Save', secondary: 'Cancel' }) // true
```

---
# Iter

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/iter/

Lazy synchronous sequences with correct iterator closing

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as Iter from '@stopcock/fp/iter'
```

`Iter<A>` is a lazy `Iterable<A>`. Operators do no work until a terminal pulls
the sequence. Constructors in this module are repeatable; `Iter.from` reflects
the repeatability of the iterable you provide.

Iter has 25 dual operations. See every direct and curried pair in the
[complete dual-call catalogue](/api/modules#complete-dual-call-catalogue).

## Constructors

```ts
Iter.from(iterable)
Iter.fromIterator(() => iterator)
Iter.defer(() => iterable)
Iter.empty()
Iter.of(1, 2, 3)
Iter.range(0, 10, 2)
Iter.repeat(value)
Iter.iterate(seed, next)
Iter.unfold(seed, step)
```

`range` excludes its end. `repeat` and `iterate` are infinite; pair them with a
bounded terminal such as `take`.

## Transformations

The core lazy vocabulary includes:

```ts
Iter.map(f)
Iter.filter(predicate)
Iter.filterMap(f)
Iter.flatMap(f)
Iter.flatten
Iter.tap(effect)
Iter.take(count)
Iter.drop(count)
Iter.takeWhile(predicate)
Iter.dropWhile(predicate)
Iter.scan(reducer, initial)
Iter.chunk(size)
Iter.intersperse(separator)
Iter.distinct
Iter.distinctBy(key)
Iter.concat(other)
Iter.zip(other)
Iter.zipWith(other, combine)
```

Transformations are usable directly or in `pipe`:

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'

const doubled = Iter.map([1, 2, 3], (value) => value * 2)
const doubledInPipe = pipe(
  [1, 2, 3],
  Iter.map((value) => value * 2),
)

const result = pipe(
  Iter.range(1, Infinity),
  Iter.filter((value) => value % 2 === 0),
  Iter.map((value) => value * value),
  Iter.take(3),
  Iter.toArray,
)
// [4, 16, 36]
```

## Terminals

```ts
Iter.toArray(source)
Iter.toArrayInto(source, target)
pipe(source, Iter.toArrayInto(target))
Iter.reduce(source, reducer, initial)
pipe(source, Iter.reduce(reducer, initial))
Iter.forEach(source, effect)
pipe(source, Iter.forEach(effect))
Iter.first(source) // Option<A>
Iter.last(source) // Option<A>
Iter.find(source, predicate) // Option<A>
pipe(source, Iter.find(predicate)) // Option<A>
Iter.some(source, predicate)
pipe(source, Iter.some(predicate))
Iter.every(source, predicate)
pipe(source, Iter.every(predicate))
Iter.count(source)
```

Partial terminals return `Option`; absence is never encoded as an ambiguous
`undefined`.

## Resource safety

Short-circuiting operations call `return()` on an upstream iterator when it is
still open. This matters for generators that own file handles, cursors, or
other resources:

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'

function* rows() {
  try {
    yield* databaseCursor
  } finally {
    databaseCursor.close()
  }
}

pipe(rows(), Iter.take(10), Iter.toArray)
```

The `finally` block runs after the tenth value.

---
# Map and Record

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/keyed/

Keyed lookups, lazy defaults, and when to reach for Record over Object

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as MapOps from '@stopcock/fp/map'
import * as Record from '@stopcock/fp/record'
```

Map and Record expose 42 dual operations between them. The [complete dual-call
catalogue](/api/modules#complete-dual-call-catalogue) lists both shapes of each
operation.

## Reading a key

Three lookups, three different answers to "what if it is not there?":

```ts
MapOps.get(scores, 'ada') // Option<number>
pipe(scores, MapOps.get('ada')) // Option<number>
MapOps.getOrUndefined(scores, 'ada') // number | undefined
pipe(scores, MapOps.getOrUndefined('ada')) // number | undefined
MapOps.getOrElse(scores, 'ada', () => 0) // number
pipe(
  scores,
  MapOps.getOrElse('ada', () => 0),
) // number
```

`getOrElse` is lazy. The fallback runs at most once, and only when the key is
genuinely absent, so an expensive default costs nothing on a hit:

```ts
const directConfig = MapOps.getOrElse(cache, url, () => parseExpensiveDefault())
const pipedConfig = pipe(
  cache,
  MapOps.getOrElse(url, () => parseExpensiveDefault()),
)
```

A key whose stored value is `undefined` is present. All three operations agree
on that: `get` returns `Some(undefined)`, `getOrUndefined` returns `undefined`,
and `getOrElse` returns `undefined` without calling the fallback. If you need
to tell "missing" from "stored `undefined`", use `get`.

Every lookup accepts the map first for a direct call, or curries the key first
so it drops straight into `pipe`:

```ts
pipe(
  scores,
  MapOps.getOrElse('ada', () => 0),
)
```

## Record or Object?

Both hold string- and symbol-keyed data, so the split is about what the value
means, not about the runtime shape.

Reach for `Record` when the keys are data and every value has the same type: a
lookup table, a counter, an index built at runtime. It is the cheaper contract:
it works in enumerable own properties on null-prototype objects and does not
carry descriptor, accessor, or prototype machinery.

Reach for `Object` when the keys are the _shape_: a struct with a known set of
differently-typed fields, especially when you need nested path writes, symbol
preservation, or descriptor-faithful clones.

There is no `Record` path helper. Nested writes into homogeneous data are
`Obj.setPath`'s job, and a `Record`-flavoured copy of it would be the same
traversal with a narrower type.

---
# Lens migration

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/lenses/

The 2.0 optic module replaces the old root lens helpers

The 1.x root lens helpers were replaced by the unified
`@stopcock/fp/optic` module. Import the module explicitly:

```diff
- import { prop, view, set, over } from '@stopcock/fp'
+ import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
+ import * as Optic from '@stopcock/fp/optic'

- const name = view(user, prop<User, 'name'>('name'))
+ const nameOptic = Optic.prop<User, 'name'>('name')
+ const name = Optic.view(nameOptic, user)
+ const nameInPipe = pipe(user, Optic.view(nameOptic))

- const updated = over(user, prop<User, 'name'>('name'), String.toUpperCase)
+ const updated = Optic.modify(nameOptic, user, String.toUpperCase)
+ const updatedInPipe = pipe(user, Optic.modify(nameOptic, String.toUpperCase))
```

The full-arity forms execute immediately. Omitting the source returns the same
operation as a data-last step for `pipe`.

The five dual optic operations and their exact parameter order are in the
[complete dual-call catalogue](/api/modules#complete-dual-call-catalogue).

The new module covers lenses, optionals, prisms, traversals, isomorphisms,
getters, folds, setters, keyed `At` optics, composition, a fluent builder, and
law helpers. Read the [Optic API](/api/optic).

---
# Logic migration

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/logic/

Logic was split into focused function and guard modules

The broad 1.x `Logic` namespace was removed from the 2.0 public surface.

Guard and Match now expose 13 dual operations. The [complete dual-call
catalogue](/api/modules#complete-dual-call-catalogue) lists both call shapes;
the Function utilities remain explicit function factories.

Use `@stopcock/fp/function` for function-level composition:

```ts
import * as Fn from '@stopcock/fp/function'

Fn.complement(predicate)
Fn.ifElse(predicate, onTrue, onFalse)
Fn.always(value)
```

Use `@stopcock/fp/guard` for predicate and refinement composition:

```ts
import * as G from '@stopcock/fp/guard'

const nonBlank = G.and(G.isString, G.isNonBlankString)
const stringOrNumber = G.or(G.isString, G.isNumber)
const notNullish = G.not(G.isNullish)
```

Use `@stopcock/fp/eq` for domain equality, `@stopcock/fp/match` for lightweight
tagged-data dispatch, or the full `@stopcock/pattern` companion for structural
and exhaustive pattern matching.

---
# M (Math)

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/math/

add, multiply, sum, mean, median. Arithmetic and stats for pipe

The five dual arithmetic operations appear with both shapes in the [complete
dual-call catalogue](/api/modules#complete-dual-call-catalogue).

## Single-argument

```ts
inc(n: number): number
dec(n: number): number
negate(n: number): number
product(arr: number[]): number
```

## Dual-form

```ts
add(a: number, b: number): number
add(b: number): (a: number) => number
subtract(a: number, b: number): number
subtract(b: number): (a: number) => number
multiply(a: number, b: number): number
multiply(b: number): (a: number) => number
divide(a: number, b: number): number
divide(b: number): (a: number) => number
modulo(a: number, b: number): number
modulo(b: number): (a: number) => number
```

## Examples

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as A from '@stopcock/fp/array'
import * as M from '@stopcock/fp/math'

// apply discount
pipe(prices, A.map(M.multiply(0.9))) // 10% off

// offset scores
pipe(rawScores, A.map(M.add(curve)))

// compound product
M.product([2, 3, 4]) // 24

// counter operations
pipe(count, M.inc) // count + 1
pipe(count, M.dec) // count - 1
pipe(value, M.negate) // -value

// both call shapes
M.modulo(17, 5) // 2, direct data-first
pipe(17, M.modulo(5)) // 2, curried data-last
```

---
# Module catalogue

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/modules/

Every public @stopcock/fp entrypoint

`@stopcock/fp` keeps its root small. Import specialist APIs from these stable,
tree-shakeable subpaths.

The package exposes 491 dual operations under one name per operation. The
complete catalogue below shows every direct data-first and curried data-last
shape.

## Collections and sequences

| Subpath              | Purpose                                                                                          |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `/array`             | Eager array operators, streaming steps the build-time compiler can fuse, explicit `*Into` writes |
| `/readonly-array`    | Read-only alias of the array vocabulary                                                          |
| `/non-empty-array`   | Constructors and total operations for non-empty arrays                                           |
| `/tuple`             | Typed tuple construction, mapping, zipping, and projection                                       |
| `/record`            | Homogeneous property-keyed dictionaries with one value type                                      |
| `/map`               | Immutable `Map` operations                                                                       |
| `/set`               | Immutable `Set` operations                                                                       |
| `/typed-array`       | Numeric typed-array transforms and explicit destination buffers                                  |
| `/indexed`           | Shared indexed-collection operations                                                             |
| [`/iter`](/api/iter) | Lazy synchronous sequences                                                                       |

Writable `*Into` operations preserve the concrete destination type. They
reject fixed tuples, heterogeneous or refined record destinations, and
ambiguous mutable target unions whenever mutation cannot be proven sound.

## Data and errors

| Subpath                          | Purpose                                       |
| -------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| [`/option`](/api/option)         | Explicit absence                              |
| [`/result`](/api/result)         | Fail-fast recoverable errors                  |
| [`/validation`](/api/validation) | Accumulating independent errors               |
| [`/schema`](/api/schema)         | Standard Schema V1 production and consumption |
| `/these`                         | Left, right, or both values                   |
| `/nullable`                      | Focused nullable boundary helpers             |

Asynchronous failures and asynchronous iteration are provided by
`@stopcock/async`, not duplicated in the core package.

## Algebra and comparison

| Subpath                      | Purpose                                   |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| [`/eq`](/api/algebra)        | Lawful equality relations                 |
| [`/hash`](/api/algebra)      | Composable deterministic hashing          |
| [`/ord`](/api/algebra)       | Total ordering instances                  |
| `/ordering`                  | Primitive ordering values and combinators |
| [`/semigroup`](/api/algebra) | Associative combination                   |
| [`/monoid`](/api/algebra)    | Combination with an identity              |
| [`/group`](/api/algebra)     | Combination with inversion                |

## Functions and data transformation

| Subpath                | Purpose                                                                                           |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/function`            | Composition, currying, memoization, predicates, and function utilities                            |
| `/guard`               | Structural guards and refinements                                                                 |
| `/object`              | Immutable object/path operations                                                                  |
| `/string`              | String transforms and predicates                                                                  |
| `/number`              | Numeric predicates, statistics, and safe partials                                                 |
| `/math`                | Arithmetic pipeline operators                                                                     |
| `/boolean`             | Boolean combinators                                                                               |
| `/compile`             | `compile`/`compilePure` markers the build-time compiler recognizes; uncompiled, they alias `pipe` |
| `/fusion`              | Same `pipe`/`flow`/`compile`, imported by a name that says "I mean fusion"                        |
| `/fusion/debug`        | `explain`/`explainPure`; always report `'sequential'` at runtime                                  |
| [`/optic`](/api/optic) | Lenses, optionals, prisms, traversals, and more                                                   |
| `/match`               | Exhaustive tagged-value matching                                                                  |

## Functional models

| Subpath      | Purpose                               |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------- |
| `/reader`    | Environment-dependent computations    |
| `/state-fn`  | Pure state transitions                |
| `/writer`    | Values paired with accumulated output |
| `/recursion` | Stack-safe recursion schemes          |

The package export map is generated from one checked-in manifest. CI builds and
imports every runtime and declaration entry from a real packed tarball, so this
catalogue cannot silently advertise a missing module.

## Complete dual-call catalogue

This catalogue covers all 491 distinct public dual operations. The
`@stopcock/fp/readonly-array` subpath re-exports the 128 `array` operations,
so it uses the same call pairs rather than duplicating them below.

Parameter names and grouping come from the public overloads. Arguments whose
types are optional may be omitted. Staged functions keep each parenthesized
application visible, and type-only capacity proofs used by `*Into` operations
are not runtime arguments.
